1,6: So he prayed, and Apollo heard him. The god came down furious from the peaks of Olympus, with his bow and quiver on his shoulder. The arrows rattled on his back from the rage shaking him. He sat down apart from the ships with a face as dark as night. Then he shot an arrow among them, and his silver bow rang out with death. He hit the mules and the dogs first. Soon he aimed his shafts at the people themselves, and the pyres of the dead burned all day long.
1,16: Achilles glared at him and answered, “You are steeped in insolence and greed. How can any Achaean obey you, whether on a raid or in open battle? I did not come here to fight because of any wrong the Trojans did me. I have no quarrel with them. They have never driven off my cattle or my horses, or cut down my crops on the rich soil of Phthia. A great distance lies between them and me, with mountains and the roaring sea. We followed you, Sir Insolence, to please you, not ourselves. We came to win satisfaction from the Trojans for your shameless self and for Menelaus. You forget all this. Now you threaten to rob me of the prize I worked for, which the sons of the Achaeans gave me. When the Achaeans sack some rich Trojan city, I never get a prize as good as yours, even though my hands do the greater part of the fighting. When the sharing comes, your share is by far the biggest. And I, naturally, go back to my ships with whatever I can get, and I must be grateful, once the labor of fighting is over. Now I am going back to Phthia. It is far better for me to sail home with my ships. I will not stay here dishonored, piling up gold and wealth for you.”
1,18: The son of Peleus was furious. In his shaggy chest his heart was torn between two choices. He could draw his sword, push the others aside and kill the son of Atreus. Or he could hold himself back and check his anger. While he was in two minds, and was already drawing his mighty sword from its sheath, Athena came down from heaven. Hera had sent her, out of her love for both men. She seized the son of Peleus by his yellow hair. Only he could see her, and none of the others. Achilles turned in amazement, and from the fire flashing in her eyes he knew at once that she was Athena. “Why have you come,” he said, “daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus? To see the arrogance of Agamemnon, son of Atreus? Let me tell you—and it will certainly happen—he will pay for this insolence with his life.”
1,22: But the son of Peleus began abusing the son of Atreus again, for he was still in a rage. “Drunkard,” he cried, “with the face of a dog and the heart of a deer! You never dare to arm and go out to fight with the army, or to join our chosen men in an ambush. You shrink from that as you do from death itself. You would much rather go around and rob any man who speaks against you of his prize. You feed on your people, because you are king over a feeble folk. Otherwise, son of Atreus, this would be the last time you insulted anyone. So I tell you, and I swear it with a great oath. By this scepter of mine—which will never sprout leaf or shoot, nor bud again, from the day it left its stem in the mountains, since the axe stripped it of leaf and bark, and now the sons of the Achaeans carry it as judges and guardians of the laws of heaven—as surely as this, I swear that one day they will long for Achilles and not find him. On the day of your distress, when your men fall dying under the murderous hand of Hector, you will not know how to help them. You will tear your heart with rage that you insulted the bravest of the Achaeans.”
1,31: Patroclus did what his dear comrade had told him. He brought Briseis out of the tent and gave her to the heralds, who took her with them to the ships of the Achaeans—and the woman did not want to go. Then Achilles went off alone to the shore of the hoary sea. He wept and looked out over the boundless waste of waters. Raising his hands, he prayed to his immortal mother. “Mother,” he cried, “you bore me doomed to live only a short season. Surely Zeus, who thunders from Olympus, could have made that short life glorious. He has not. Agamemnon, son of Atreus, has dishonored me and taken my prize from me by force.”
2,22: “King Agamemnon, the Achaeans are about to make you a byword among all mankind. They have forgotten the promise they made you when they set out from Argos, that you would not return until you had sacked the town of Troy. Like children or widowed women, they murmur and want to set off for home. It is true that they have had toil enough to lose heart. A man grows restless at being away from his wife even for a single month, when he is on shipboard at the mercy of wind and sea. But we have now been kept here nine long years. So I cannot blame the Achaeans for turning restive. Still, we will be shamed if we go home empty-handed after so long a stay. Therefore, my friends, be patient a little longer, so that we may learn whether the prophecies of Calchas were false or true.
2,48: Thoas, son of Andraemon, commanded the Aetolians, who lived in Pleuron, Olenus, Pylene, Chalcis by the sea, and rocky Calydon, for the great king Oeneus now had no sons living and was himself dead, as was golden-haired Meleager, who had been set over the Aetolians as their king. Forty ships came with Thoas.
2,55: And those who held Pherae by the Boebean lake, with Boebe, Glaphyrae and the populous city of Iolcus, with their eleven ships, were led by Eumelus, son of Admetus, whom Alcestis bore to him. She was the loveliest of the daughters of Pelias.
2,60: Guneus brought twenty-two ships from Cyphus. The Enienes and the valiant Peraebi followed him. They lived around wintry Dodona and held the lands around the lovely river Titaresius, which sends its waters into the Peneus. The Titaresius does not mingle with the silver eddies of the Peneus but flows on top of them like oil, because it is a branch of dread Orcus and of the river Styx.
3,5: Then Hector scolded him. “Paris,” he said, “you evil-hearted Paris, so fair to look at, so mad for women, such a liar. I wish you had never been born, or had died unmarried. That would be better than living to be disgraced and looked at sideways. Will the Achaeans not mock us? They will say we sent a champion who is fair to look at but has no brains and no courage. Did you not, being what you are, gather your followers and sail over the seas? Did you not, from a far country, carry off a lovely woman married among a people of warriors—bringing sorrow to your father, your city and your whole country, joy to your enemies, and a hang-dog shame to yourself? And now you do not dare face Menelaus and find out what kind of man he is, whose wife you have stolen? Where would your lyre be then, and your love-tricks, your handsome locks and your fair looks, when you were lying in the dust in front of him? The Trojans are a weak-kneed people. Otherwise you would long ago have been given a shirt of stones for the wrongs you have done them.”
3,19: Antenor then said, “Madam, you have spoken truly. Odysseus once came here as an envoy about you, and Menelaus came with him. I received them in my own house, so I know both of them by sight and by conversation. When they stood up before the assembled Trojans, Menelaus had the broader shoulders, but when both were seated Odysseus looked the more royal. After a time they delivered their message. The speech of Menelaus ran trippingly off the tongue. He did not say much, being a man of few words, but he spoke very clearly and to the point, though he was the younger of the two. Odysseus, on the other hand, when he rose to speak, was at first silent and kept his eyes fixed on the ground. He made no play or graceful movement with his scepter. He held it straight and stiff, like a man unpracticed in oratory, and you might have taken him for a mere churl or simpleton. But when he raised his voice and the words came driving from his deep chest like winter snow before the wind, no one could touch him, and nobody thought any more about how he looked.”
4,24: So the old man instructed them, for he had been in many a fight, and King Agamemnon was glad. “I wish,” he said to him, “that your limbs were as supple and your strength as sure as your judgment. But age, the common enemy of mankind, has laid its hand on you. I wish it had fallen on some other man, and that you were still young.”
4,33: As when a mighty wave thunders on the beach after the west wind has whipped it into fury, and has reared its head far out and now comes crashing down on the shore, bowing its arching crest high over the jagged rocks and spewing salt foam in all directions, in just that way the close-packed ranks of the Danaans marched steadily to battle. The chiefs gave orders, each to his own people, but the men said not a word. No one would have thought it possible: huge as the host was, it seemed there was not a tongue among them, so silent were they in their obedience. As they marched, the armor on their bodies glistened in the sun. The noise of the Trojan ranks was different. It was like the sound of many thousand ewes standing in the yards of some rich flock-master, waiting to be milked, and bleating without pause as they answer their lambs. The Trojans had no single speech or language. Their tongues were mixed, and they came from many different places. Ares drove these on, and Athena the others. With them came Panic, Rout, and Strife, whose fury never tires, sister and friend of murderous Ares. She is small at first, but she grows until she lifts her head to heaven while her feet are still on earth. She was the one who went among them and threw down discord, to the increase of sorrow, with an even hand between the two sides.
5,18: The son of Lycaon answered, “Aeneas, I take him to be none other than the son of Tydeus. I know him by his shield, by the visor of his helmet and by his horses. He may be a god, but if he is the man I say he is, he is not making all this havoc without heaven’s help. Some god stands by his side, shrouded in a cloud of darkness, and that god turned my arrow aside when it had hit him. I have already shot at him and hit him on the right shoulder. My arrow went through the breast-piece of his cuirass, and I felt sure I had sent him hurrying to the world below. But it seems I have not killed him, so there must be a god who is angry with me. On top of that, I have neither horse nor chariot. In my father’s stables there are eleven excellent chariots, fresh from the builder and quite new, with cloths spread over them, and beside each one stands a pair of horses, champing barley and rye. My old father Lycaon urged me again and again, when I was at home and about to set out, to take chariots and horses with me so that I could lead the Trojans in battle. I would not listen to him. It would have been much better if I had. But I was thinking of the horses, which were used to eating their fill, and I was afraid they would go short of food in such a great gathering of men. So I left them at home and came on foot to Ilium, armed only with my bow and arrows. It seems these are of no use, for I have already hit two chieftains, the sons of Atreus and of Tydeus, and although I certainly drew blood, I have only made them more furious. I did wrong to take my bow down from its peg on the day I led my band of Trojans to Ilium in Hector’s service. If I ever get home again and see my native place, my wife and my great house, may someone cut my head off then and there if I do not break this bow and put it on a hot fire. Those are the tricks it plays on me.”
5,29: Meanwhile the son of Tydeus was chasing the Cyprian goddess with his spear in hand. He knew she was weak, not one of those goddesses who have power over men in battle, like Athena or Enyo, the waster of cities. After a long chase he caught up with her, lunged, and thrust his spear into the flesh of her delicate hand. The point ripped through the ambrosial robe that the Graces had woven for her and pierced the skin between her wrist and the palm of her hand. The immortal blood, or ichor, that runs in the veins of the blessed gods came pouring from the wound. The gods do not eat bread or drink wine, and so they have no blood like ours, and that is why they are immortal. Aphrodite screamed and dropped her son, but Phoebus Apollo caught him in his arms and hid him in a cloud of darkness, so that no Danaan could drive a spear into his chest and kill him. As he left her, Diomedes shouted, “Daughter of Zeus, leave war and battle alone. Is it not enough for you to deceive silly women? If you meddle in fighting, you will get something that makes you shudder at the very name of war.”
5,32: Laughter-loving Aphrodite answered, “Proud Diomedes, the son of Tydeus, wounded me because I was carrying my dear son Aeneas, whom I love best of all mankind, out of the fight. This war is no longer just between Trojans and Achaeans. The Danaans are now fighting with the immortals.”
5,52: His comrades carried Sarpedon out of the fight. He was in great pain from the weight of the spear dragging in his wound. They were in such haste and distress as they carried him that no one thought to pull the spear out of his thigh so that he could walk upright. Meanwhile the Achaeans carried off the body of Tlepolemus. Odysseus was moved to pity and panted for the fight as he watched them. He could not decide whether to go after the son of Zeus or to slaughter the rank and file of the Lycians. It was not fated that he should kill the son of Zeus, so Athena turned him against the main body of the Lycians. He killed Coeranus, Alastor, Chromius, Alcandrus, Halius, Noemon, and Prytanis, and he would have killed more, but great Hector noticed him. Hector, dressed in his suit of mail, hurried to the front of the fight and filled the Danaans with terror. Sarpedon was glad to see him coming and begged him, “Son of Priam, do not let me lie here and fall into the hands of the Danaans. Help me. And since I am not to return home and gladden the hearts of my wife and my infant son, let me die inside the walls of your city.”
6,13: The son of Hippolochus answered, “Son of Tydeus, why do you ask about my family line? Men come and go like the leaves on the trees from year to year. The wind scatters the autumn leaves on the ground, but when spring returns the forest bursts into bud with fresh vines. It is the same with the generations of mankind: the new spring up as the old pass away. But if you want to know my descent, many people know it well. There is a city in the heart of Argos, pasture land of horses, called Ephyra. Sisyphus lived there, the craftiest of all mankind. He was the son of Aeolus, and he had a son named Glaucus, who was the father of Bellerophon. Heaven gave Bellerophon the most surpassing good looks and beauty. But Proetus plotted his ruin. Proetus was the stronger, and he drove Bellerophon out of the land of the Argives, over which Zeus had made Proetus ruler. The reason was that Antea, the wife of Proetus, lusted after Bellerophon and wanted him to lie with her in secret. Bellerophon was an honorable man and refused, so she told lies about him to Proetus. ‘Proetus,’ she said, ‘kill Bellerophon or die yourself, for he wanted to lie with me against my will.’ The king was angry, but he shrank from killing Bellerophon. Instead he sent him to Lycia with lying letters of introduction, written on a folded tablet and full of ill against the man who carried it. He told Bellerophon to show these letters to his father-in-law, so that he would die that way. Bellerophon went to Lycia, and the gods escorted him safely.
6,21: His mother went into the house and called her waiting-women, and they gathered the matrons from all over the city. Then she went down to her fragrant storeroom, where her embroidered robes were kept. These were the work of Sidonian women, whom Paris had brought over from Sidon when he sailed the seas on the voyage during which he carried off Helen. Hecuba took out the largest robe, the one most beautifully rich with embroidery, to give to Athena. It glittered like a star and lay at the very bottom of the chest. She set off with it, and many matrons went with her.
6,23: While they were praying to the daughter of great Zeus, Hector went to the fine house of Paris. The foremost builders in the land had built it for him: a house, storehouse, and courtyard near those of Priam and Hector on the acropolis. Hector went in, holding a spear eleven cubits long. Its bronze point gleamed ahead of him, fastened to the shaft by a ring of gold. He found Paris inside the house, busy with his armor, his shield and cuirass, and handling his curved bow. Argive Helen sat there too with her women, giving them their various tasks. When Hector saw Paris, he rebuked him with words of scorn. “Sir,” he said, “you do wrong to nurse this bitterness. The people are dying as they fight around this town of ours. You would blame anyone else you saw shirking his part in the fight. Up, then, or before long the city will be in flames.”
7,18: With those words Hector lifted his spear and hurled it. It hit the sevenfold shield on its outermost layer, the eighth, which was bronze. The spear tore through six layers of the shield, but it stuck in the seventh hide. Then Ajax threw. He struck the round shield of the son of Priam, and the terrible spear drove through the gleaming shield and on through the finely worked cuirass. It cut the shirt along Hector’s side, but he swerved, and that saved his life. Each man pulled his spear out of the shield, and they crashed together like savage lions, or like wild boars of great strength and endurance. The son of Priam hit the middle of Ajax’s shield, but the bronze did not break, and the point of his spear bent back. Then Ajax sprang forward and drove his spear through Hector’s shield. It went right through and checked Hector as he lunged to attack, and it gashed his neck, so that blood poured from the wound. Even so Hector kept on fighting. He gave ground and grabbed a huge, rugged stone that lay on the plain with his strong hand. With this he hit the boss in the middle of Ajax’s shield, and the bronze rang out. But Ajax snatched up a far larger stone, swung it high, and hurled it with enormous force. That stone, as big as a millstone, smashed Hector’s shield inward and threw him on his back, with the shield crushing him beneath it. Apollo lifted him up at once. They would then have hacked at each other with their swords in close combat, if the heralds, messengers of gods and men, had not come forward, one from the Trojans and one from the Achaeans. These were Talthybius and Idaeus, both honorable men. They parted the two men with their staves, and the good herald Idaeus said, “My sons, stop fighting. You are both brave men, and both are dear to Zeus. We all know that. But night is falling, and it is good to give way when night commands.”
8,15: With these words he turned the horses back through the thick of the battle. With a cry that tore the air, the Trojans and Hector showered their missiles after them. Hector shouted to Diomedes, “Son of Tydeus, until now the Danaans have honored you with a place at table, with meals, and with cups filled with wine. From now on they will despise you, because you have become no better than a woman. Get out, you girl and coward! You will never climb our walls through any flinching on my part, and you will never carry off our wives in your ships. I will kill you with my own hand.”
9,1: The Trojans kept watch. But Panic, the comrade of blood-stained Rout, had taken a firm hold on the Achaeans, and all their princes were in despair. As when the two winds that blow from Thrace, the north wind and the northwest wind, spring up suddenly and stir the sea to fury, and at once the dark waves lift their heads and scatter seaweed in every direction, so were the hearts of the Achaeans troubled.
9,20: “As for him, the hound does not even dare to look me in the face. I will not sit in council with him, and I will have no share in any plan of his. He has wronged and deceived me enough. He will not cheat me a second time. Let him go his own way, since Zeus has taken away his reason. I hate his presents, and I do not care a straw for the man himself. Let him offer ten times what he has offered now, or twenty—no, not even if he gave me everything he owns in the world, now or ever. Let him promise me the wealth of Orchomenus or of Egyptian Thebes, the richest city in the whole world, which has a hundred gates, and through each gate two hundred men can drive out at once with their chariots and horses. Let him offer gifts as many as the sands of the sea or the dust of the plain. Even so he will not move me until I have paid him back in full for the bitter wrong he did me. I will not marry his daughter. She could be as beautiful as Aphrodite and as skilled as Athena, and I would still have none of her. Let some other man take her, one who suits her better and rules a larger kingdom. If the gods bring me safely home, Peleus himself will find me a wife. There are Achaean women in Hellas and Phthia, daughters of kings who rule cities, and I can take whichever of them I like and marry her. Many times, back home in Phthia, I longed to court a wife who would suit me and to enjoy the riches of my old father Peleus. My life is worth more to me than all the wealth of Ilium in the days when it was at peace, before the Achaeans came, or than all the treasure that lies on the stone floor of Apollo’s temple under the cliffs of Pytho. Cattle and sheep can be won by raiding, and a man can buy tripods and horses if he wants them. But once a man’s life has left him, it can be neither bought nor raided back.
9,22: They all stayed silent, shaken by how harshly he had refused them. At last the old knight Phoenix, in his great fear for the ships of the Achaeans, burst into tears and spoke. “Noble Achilles, if you are really set on going home, and your fierce anger will not let you do anything to save the ships from burning, then how can I stay here without you, my son? Your father Peleus sent me with you on the day he sent you from Phthia to Agamemnon, when you were only a boy. You knew nothing yet of war, or of the skills that make men known in council. He sent me to train you in every excellence of speech and action. So, my son, I will not stay here without you—no, not even if heaven itself were to strip the years from me and make me as young as I was when I first left Hellas, the land of fair women. I was running from the anger of my father Amyntor, son of Ormenus. He was furious with me over his concubine, whom he loved, to the wrong of his wife, my mother. My mother begged me without stopping to sleep with the woman myself, so that she would come to hate my father, and in time I gave in. But my father soon found out, and cursed me bitterly, calling the dreadful Erinyes to witness. He prayed that no son of mine would ever sit on his knees—and the gods, Zeus of the world below and awful Proserpine, fulfilled his curse. I made up my mind to kill him, but some god held back my rashness. He made me think of what men’s evil tongues would say, and how I would be branded the murderer of my father. Even so, I could not bear to stay in my father’s house with him so bitter against me. My cousins and kinsmen gathered around me and pressed me hard to stay. They slaughtered many sheep and many oxen, set many fat hogs to roast before the fire, and broached many jars of my father’s wine. For nine whole nights they set a guard over me, taking turns to watch, and they kept a fire burning always, both in the cloister of the outer court and in the inner court at the doors of the room where I lay. But when the darkness of the tenth night came, I broke through the closed doors of my room and climbed the wall of the outer court, after slipping quickly and unseen through the guards and the women servants. Then I fled through Hellas until I came to fertile Phthia, mother of sheep, and to King Peleus. He welcomed me and treated me as a father treats an only son who will inherit all his wealth. He made me rich and put me over many people, setting me on the borders of Phthia, where I ruled as chief over the Dolopians.
9,25: “As long as Meleager was in the field, things went badly for the Curetes, and for all their numbers they could not hold their ground under the city walls. But in time Meleager grew angry, as even a wise man sometimes will. He was enraged at his mother Althaea, and so he stayed at home with his wedded wife, fair Cleopatra. She was the daughter of Marpessa daughter of Euenus, and of Ides, the man who was then alive. This Ides took up his bow and faced King Apollo himself for the sake of fair Marpessa. After that, her father and mother named her Alcyone, because her mother had cried out in grief like the halcyon bird when Phoebus Apollo carried her off. So Meleager stayed at home with Cleopatra, feeding the anger he felt over his mother’s curses. His mother was grieving for her brother’s death. She prayed to the gods and beat the earth with her hands, calling on Hades and on awful Proserpine. She was on her knees, and her bosom was wet with tears, as she prayed that they would kill her son. And Erinys, who walks in darkness and knows no pity, heard her from Erebus.
10,1: All the other princes of the Achaeans slept soundly through the night, but Agamemnon son of Atreus was troubled and could find no rest. As when the husband of fair Hera flashes his lightning as a sign of heavy rain, or hail, or a snowfall that turns the ground white, or else as a sign that he will open the wide jaws of hungry war, so Agamemnon heaved many a heavy sigh, for his soul trembled within him. When he looked out over the plain of Troy, he marveled at the many watchfires burning in front of Ilium, and at the sound of pipes and flutes and the hum of men. But when he turned toward the ships and the armies of the Achaeans, he tore his hair out by handfuls before Zeus on high, and groaned aloud, so uneasy was his soul. In the end he decided it was best to go at once to Nestor son of Neleus, and see whether the two of them could find some way to save the Achaeans from destruction. So he got up, put on his shirt, tied his sandals on his comely feet, threw over his shoulders the skin of a huge tawny lion—a skin that reached his feet—and took his spear in his hand.
10,33: Dolon answered, his legs shaking under him. “Hector lured me away from my better judgment with his empty, flattering promises. He said he would give me the horses of the noble son of Peleus and his chariot decked with bronze. He told me to go through the darkness of the fleeting night, get close to the enemy, and find out whether the ships are still guarded as before, or whether the Achaeans, now that we have beaten them, plan to flee and are neglecting their watches out of sheer exhaustion.”
10,37: “I will tell you everything truthfully,” replied Dolon. “Toward the sea lie the Carians, the Paeonian bowmen, the Leleges, the Cauconians and the noble Pelasgi. The Lycians, the proud Mysians, the Phrygians and the Meonians have their place on the side toward Thymbra. But why ask about all this? If you want to find a way into the Trojan host, there are the Thracians, who have only just arrived. They lie apart from the others at the far end of the camp, and their king is Rhesus son of Eioneus. His horses are the finest and strongest I have ever seen. They are whiter than snow and swifter than any wind. His chariot is decked with silver and gold, and he has brought his marvelous golden armor, of the rarest workmanship. It is too splendid for any mortal man to wear and fit only for the gods. Now take me to the ships, or tie me up securely here until you come back and have tested my words to see whether they are false or true.”
10,39: Dolon was reaching for his beard to plead with him further, but Diomedes struck him with his sword in the middle of the neck and cut through both sinews, so that his head fell rolling in the dust while he was still speaking. They took the ferret-skin cap from his head, and the wolf skin, the bow and the long spear. Odysseus hung them up aloft in honor of Athena, goddess of plunder, and prayed, “Accept these, goddess. We give them to you before all the gods on Olympus. Now guide us further, to the horses and the sleeping place of the Thracians.”
10,47: Odysseus answered, “Nestor son of Neleus, honor of the Achaean name, heaven, if it so wills, can give us even better horses than these, for the gods are far mightier than we are. But the horses you ask about have just come from Thrace. Diomedes killed their king along with the twelve bravest of his companions. Close by the ships we took a thirteenth man, a scout whom Hector and the other Trojans had sent to spy on our ships.”
11,16: When noble Coon, Antenor’s eldest son, saw this, his eyes were sore at the sight of his fallen brother. Unseen by Agamemnon, he got beside him, spear in hand, and wounded him in the middle of the arm below the elbow, so that the point of the spear went right through the arm. Agamemnon was convulsed with pain, but even so he did not leave off struggling and fighting. He grasped his spear, which flew swift as the wind, and sprang upon Coon. Coon was trying to drag off the body of his brother, his father’s son, by the foot, and was crying for help to all the bravest of his comrades. Agamemnon struck him with a bronze-shod spear and killed him as he dragged the dead body through the press of men under cover of his shield. Then, standing over the body of Iphidamas, he cut off Coon’s head. So the sons of Antenor met their fate at the hands of the son of Atreus and went down into the house of Hades.
12,1: While the son of Menoetius tended Eurypylus’s wound inside the tent, the Argives and Trojans went on fighting desperately. But the trench and the high wall above it were not going to hold the Trojans back much longer. The Achaeans had built the wall to protect their ships, and had dug the trench all around it to keep both the ships and the rich spoils they had taken safe. But they had never offered a great sacrifice to the gods. Because it was built without the immortals’ consent, it did not last. As long as Hector lived, Achilles kept up his anger, and Priam’s city stayed unsacked, the great wall of the Achaeans stood firm. Then the bravest of the Trojans died, and many of the Argives too, though some were still alive. In the tenth year the city was sacked, and the Argives sailed home to their own country. After that Poseidon and Apollo made a plan to destroy the wall. They turned the streams of all the rivers that run from Mount Ida to the sea onto it: the Rhesus, the Heptaporus, the Caresus, the Rhodius, the Grenicus, the Aesopus, and goodly Scamander, and the Simois, where many a shield and helmet had fallen and many a hero of the race of demigods had bitten the dust. Phoebus Apollo brought the mouths of all these rivers together and sent them flowing against the wall for nine days. Zeus rained the whole time, so that the wall would be washed into the sea sooner. Poseidon himself, trident in hand, looked over the work. He threw into the sea all the foundations of beams and stones that the Achaeans had laid with so much toil. He leveled everything along the mighty stream of the Hellespont, and when the wall was swept away he spread a great beach of sand over the place where it had stood. Then he turned the rivers back into their old channels.
13,15: Poseidon was exceedingly angry that his grandson Amphimachus had fallen. He went to the tents and ships of the Achaeans to urge the Danaans on still further and to devise evil for the Trojans. Idomeneus met him as he was leaving a comrade who had just come from the fight, wounded in the knee. His fellow soldiers had carried the man off the field. Idomeneus gave orders to the physicians and went on to his tent, for he was still thirsting for battle. Poseidon spoke in the likeness and with the voice of Thoas son of Andraemon, who ruled the Aetolians of all Pleuron and high Calydon and was honored among his people as if he were a god. “Idomeneus,” he said, “lawgiver to the Cretans, what has become of the threats the sons of the Achaeans used to make against the Trojans?”
13,24: At this, Meriones, peer of Ares, went to the tent and got himself a bronze spear. He followed after Idomeneus, set on great deeds of valor. As when baneful Ares goes out to battle, and his son Panic, strong and dauntless, goes with him to strike terror even into the heart of a hero—the pair have left Thrace to arm themselves among the Ephyri or the brave Phlegyans, but they will not listen to both of the contending armies, and will give victory to one side or the other—so Meriones and Idomeneus, captains of men, went out to battle in their bronze armor. Meriones spoke first. “Son of Deucalion,” he said, “where would you have us begin fighting? On the right wing of the army, in the center, or on the left wing, where I think the Achaeans will be weakest?”
13,26: Meriones, peer of swift Ares, then led the way until they came to the part of the army that Idomeneus had named.
14,2: He took the shield of his son Thrasymedes from the tent, where it lay gleaming with bronze, since Thrasymedes had taken his father’s shield. He also picked up his redoubtable bronze-shod spear. As soon as he was outside he saw the disastrous rout of the Achaeans. Their wall was overthrown, and they were fleeing in confusion before the Trojans. As when there is a heavy swell on the sea and the waves are dumb, they watch for the quarter from which the fierce winds may spring on them, but they stay where they are and roll neither this way nor that, until some particular wind sweeps down from heaven to decide for them. In the same way the old man was torn over whether to make for the crowd of Danaans or go in search of Agamemnon. In the end he thought it best to go to the son of Atreus. Meanwhile the armies kept fighting and killing one another, and the hard bronze rattled on their bodies as they thrust at each other with swords and spears.
14,23: Hera did as he asked. She swore the oath and called on all the gods of the nether world, the ones called Titans, as witnesses. When the oath was complete, the two wrapped themselves in a thick mist and hurried on, leaving Lemnos and Imbrus behind them. Soon they came to many-fountained Ida, mother of wild beasts, and to Lectum, where they left the sea and went on over land. The tops of the forest trees rustled beneath their feet. Sleep stopped here. Before Zeus could catch sight of him, he climbed a lofty pine—the tallest that lifted its head toward heaven on all Ida. He hid among the branches and sat there looking like the sweet-singing bird of the mountains, which the gods call Chalcis and men call Cymindis. Hera then went on to Gargarus, the topmost peak of Ida, and Zeus, driver of the clouds, saw her. The moment he did, he was filled with the same passionate desire for her that he had felt when they first enjoyed each other’s embraces and slept together without their dear parents knowing anything about it. He went up to her and said, “What do you want, that you have come here from Olympus, and with no chariot or horses to carry you?”
14,31: So he spoke, and they did as he said. The son of Tydeus, Odysseus, and Agamemnon, wounded though they were, put the others in order and went everywhere arranging the exchanges of armor. The most valiant took the best armor and gave the worse to the worse man. When they had put on their bronze armor, they marched on with Poseidon at their head. In his strong hand he gripped his terrible sword, sharp of edge and flashing like lightning. Woe to anyone who meets it in the day of battle; all men shake with fear and keep away from it.
15,2: The father of gods and men pitied Hector and glared at Hera. “I see it, Hera, you mischief-making trickster,” he said. “Your cunning has kept Hector from fighting and has routed his army. I am half inclined to thrash you, and you would be the first to reap the fruits of your scurvy knavery. Do you not remember the time I hung you up? I fastened two anvils to your feet and bound your hands in a golden chain that no one could break, and you dangled in mid-air among the clouds. All the gods of Olympus raged, but they could not get near enough to set you free. Any of them I caught, I seized and hurled from the heavenly threshold until he came fainting down to earth. Even that did not ease my mind of its constant anxiety about noble Heracles. You and Boreas had spitefully carried him off across the seas to Cos, after you had won the tempests over to your scheme. But I rescued him, and in spite of all his mighty labors I brought him back to Argos. I remind you of this so that you will learn to stop your deceit, and see how much you are likely to gain from the embraces you left to come here and trick me.”
15,16: Poseidon answered, “Goddess Iris, what you say is well timed. It is good when a messenger shows such discretion. Even so, it cuts me to the heart when anyone rebukes so angrily one who is his own peer and has equal power. Now, though, I will give way, in spite of my displeasure. And let me tell you something more, and I mean it: if Zeus spares steep Ilium and will not let the Achaeans have the great triumph of sacking it, against the wishes of myself, of Athena, driver of the spoil, of Hera, of Hermes, and of King Hephaestus, then let him understand that he will bring on himself our implacable resentment.”
15,24: The Trojans came on in a dense body, and Hector strode at their head. Phoebus Apollo walked in front of him, with cloud wrapped around his shoulders. In his hands he carried the terrible aegis, shaggy with fringe, that Hephaestus the smith had given to Zeus to strike terror into men’s hearts. Holding it, Apollo led the Trojans on.
16,1: So the fight went on around the ship of Protesilaus. Meanwhile Patroclus came up to Achilles with tears welling in his eyes, like a spring whose clear water spills down the ledges of a high cliff. Achilles saw him crying and felt sorry for him. He said, “Patroclus, why are you standing there in tears like a silly little girl who runs to her mother and begs to be picked up and carried? She clings to her mother’s dress and holds her back though her mother is in a hurry, and she keeps looking up at her with wet eyes until her mother lifts her. You are shedding tears just like that, Patroclus. Do you have something to tell the Myrmidons, or me? Or have you had news from Phthia that only you know? They tell me that Menoetius son of Actor is still alive, and that Peleus son of Aeacus is still alive among the Myrmidons. We two would grieve bitterly to lose either of them. Or are you mourning for the Argives, and for the way they are being killed at the ships because of their own arrogance? Do not hide anything from me. Say it, so that both of us know.”
16,2: Then, knight Patroclus, you answered with a deep sigh, “Achilles, son of Peleus, greatest champion of the Achaeans, do not be angry. I weep because of the disaster that has fallen on the Argives. Every man who has been their champion until now is lying at the ships, wounded by sword or spear. Brave Diomedes son of Tydeus has been hit by a spear. Famed Odysseus and Agamemnon have both taken sword wounds. Eurypylus has been struck in the thigh by an arrow. Skilled healers are tending these heroes and curing their wounds. And you, Achilles, are you still so unyielding? May I never carry the kind of rage you carry, to the ruin of your own good name. Who in later stories will speak well of you if you do not save the Argives from destruction now? You have no pity. The knight Peleus was not your father, and Thetis was not your mother. The gray sea bore you and the sheer cliffs gave you life, so cruel and hard are you. But perhaps you are holding back because you know of some oracle, or because your mother Thetis has told you something from the mouth of Zeus. If so, at least send me out, and the Myrmidons with me, in case I can bring the Danaans some relief. And let me wear your armor. The Trojans may take me for you and leave the field, and the hard-pressed sons of the Achaeans can get a chance to breathe. They have hardly had one while fighting. We are fresh, and we could easily drive these tired men back from our ships and tents to their own city.”
16,8: Meanwhile Achilles went everywhere among the tents and told his Myrmidons to put on their armor. As fierce, ravening wolves feast on a horned stag they have killed in the mountains, with their jaws red with blood, then go in a pack to lap water from a clear spring with their long thin tongues, reeking of blood and slaughter, and know no fear because hunger drives them, in the same way the leaders and counselors of the Myrmidons gathered around the good squire of the swift descendant of Aeacus, and Achilles himself stood among them, urging on both men and horses.
16,12: In front of them all, two men armed themselves—Patroclus and Automedon—two men with one mind, to lead the Myrmidons. Then Achilles went into his tent and opened the lid of the strong chest that silver-footed Thetis had given him to take on board ship, and had filled with shirts, cloaks against the cold, and good thick rugs. In this chest he kept a cup of rare workmanship. No man but himself might drink from it, and he made offerings from it to no god except father Zeus. He took the cup from the chest and cleansed it with sulphur. Then he rinsed it in clean water, washed his hands, and drew wine. He stood in the middle of the court and prayed, looking toward heaven and pouring out the wine as a drink offering. Zeus, whose joy is in thunder, did not fail to see him. “King Zeus,” he cried, “lord of Dodona, god of the Pelasgi, you who live far away and rule wintry Dodona, where your prophets the Selli live around you with unwashed feet and beds made on the ground—you heard me when I prayed to you before, and honored me by sending disaster on the Achaeans. Now grant me the fulfillment of one more prayer. I will stay here where my ships are lying, but I am sending my comrade into battle at the head of many Myrmidons. Grant, all-seeing Zeus, that victory goes with him. Put your courage into his heart, so that Hector learns whether my squire is man enough to fight alone, or whether his might is unbeatable only when I myself enter the turmoil of war. Afterward, when he has driven the fighting and the battle cry away from the ships, grant that he returns unharmed, with his armor and his comrades, fighters in close combat.”
16,24: Patroclus kept steering his horses toward wherever he saw the most men fleeing in confusion, cheering on his men as he went. Chariots were being smashed in all directions, and many a man tumbled from his own car and fell beneath the wheels of Patroclus’s chariot. Its immortal horses, which the gods had given to Peleus, sprang over the trench in a single bound as they raced on. Patroclus was set on getting near Hector, for he had his heart fixed on spearing him, but Hector’s horses were now hurrying him away. The whole dark earth bows before a tempest on an autumn day, when Zeus rains his hardest to punish men who give crooked judgments in their courts, drive justice out of them and ignore the decrees of heaven. All the rivers run full, the torrents tear many a new channel as they roar headlong from the mountains to the dark sea, and it goes badly for the works of men. Such was the stress and strain of the Trojan horses in their flight.
17,4: As he spoke he struck Menelaus squarely on the shield, but the spear did not go through, because the shield bent its point back. Then Menelaus took aim and prayed to father Zeus. Euphorbus was drawing back, and Menelaus struck him at the base of the throat, leaning his whole weight on the spear to drive it home. The point went straight through his neck. He fell heavily to the ground, and his armor clattered around him. His hair, which was like the hair of the Graces, and his locks so neatly bound in bands of silver and gold, were all soaked with blood. Think of a man who has grown a fine young olive tree in a clear place with plenty of water. The plant is full of promise, and though the winds beat on it from every direction, it keeps putting out its white blossoms, until the blasts of some fierce hurricane sweep down and level it with the ground. In the same way Menelaus stripped the fair youth Euphorbus of his armor after he had killed him. Or think of a fierce lion on the mountains, proud of his strength, who fastens on the finest heifer in a herd as it feeds. First he breaks her neck with his strong jaws, and then he gorges on her blood and entrails. Dogs and shepherds raise a hue and cry against him, but they keep their distance and will not come close, for they are pale with fear. In the same way no one had the courage to face valiant Menelaus. The son of Atreus would then have carried off the armor of the son of Panthous with ease, if Phoebus Apollo had not been angry. In the form of Mentes, chief of the Cicons, Apollo urged Hector to attack him. “Hector,” he said, “you are chasing after the horses of the noble son of Aeacus, but you will not take them. A mortal man cannot hold them in hand and drive them, except Achilles, whose mother is immortal. Meanwhile Menelaus son of Atreus has stood over the body of Patroclus and killed the noblest of the Trojans, Euphorbus son of Panthous, so that he can fight no more.”
17,35: Now the fierce, groaning fight raged again around Patroclus, because Athena had come down from heaven and stirred up its fury. Far-seeing Zeus, who had changed his mind, had commanded her and sent her to encourage the Danaans. Just as Zeus bends his bright bow in heaven as a sign to mankind of either war or the chill storms that keep men from their work and plague their flocks, in the same way, wrapped in such radiant raiment, Athena went into the host and spoke to each man in turn. First she took the form and voice of Phoenix and spoke to Menelaus son of Atreus, who was standing near her. “Menelaus,” she said, “it will be a shame and a dishonor to you if dogs tear apart the noble comrade of Achilles under the walls of Troy. So stand firm, and urge your men to do the same.”
18,23: “Think carefully, my friends. I urge you to go back to your city now and not wait here by the ships until morning, for we are far from our walls. As long as this man was at enmity with Agamemnon, the Achaeans were easier to deal with, and I would gladly have camped by the ships, hoping to take them. But now I am in great fear of the swift son of Peleus. He is so daring that he will never wait here on the plain, where Trojans and Achaeans fight with equal valor. He will try to storm our city and carry off our women. So do as I say, and let us retreat. This is what will happen. The darkness of night will hold the son of Peleus back for a while. But if he finds us here in the morning when he sallies out in full armor, we shall come to know him in good earnest. Glad will be the man who can escape and get back to Ilium, and many a Trojan will become meat for dogs and vultures—may I never live to hear it. If we do as I say, little as we may like it, we shall have strength in counsel during the night, and the great gates with the doors that close them will protect the city. At dawn we can arm and take our stand on the walls. He will regret it then if he sallies from the ships to fight us. He will go back when he has let his horses run their fill, driven in every direction under our walls, and he will have no mind to try to force his way into the city. Nor will he ever sack it. The dogs will devour him first.”
19,1: Saffron-robed Dawn was rising from the streams of Oceanus to bring light to mortals and immortals when Thetis reached the ships, carrying the armor the god had given her. She found her son lying across the body of Patroclus, weeping bitterly. Many of his followers were weeping around him too. The goddess walked in among them and took his hand in hers. “My son,” she said, “however much we grieve, we must let this man lie. It was heaven’s will that he fell. Now take this rich and beautiful armor from Hephaestus. No man has ever yet carried it on his shoulders.”
19,22: She wept as she spoke, and the women joined in her lament. They seemed to cry for Patroclus, but in truth each was weeping for her own sorrows. The elders of the Achaeans gathered around Achilles and begged him to eat. He groaned and refused. “I beg you,” he said, “if any comrade will listen to me, do not tell me to eat or drink. I am weighed down with grief, and I will stay fasting until the sun goes down.”
20,21: Next it was Achilles’s turn to throw. His spear struck the round shield of Aeneas right at the rim, where the bronze was thinnest, and the spear of Pelian ash went clean through. The shield rang under the blow. Aeneas was afraid. He crouched backward and held the shield out away from his body. The spear flew over his back and stuck quivering in the ground, after piercing both rings of the shield that sheltered him. Aeneas had avoided it, but he stood rooted, blinded by fear and grief, because the weapon had come so close. Then Achilles sprang at him in fury, with a deadly cry and his sharp sword drawn. Aeneas picked up a great stone, so huge that two men of today could not have lifted it, though Aeneas swung it easily by himself.
21,2: At once the hero leaned his spear against a tamarisk bush and left it on the bank. Armed with his sword alone, he plunged into the river like a god. His purpose was grim, and he hewed the Trojans down on every side. They groaned horribly as they died under the sword, and the river ran red with blood. As fish flee in fear from a huge dolphin and fill every nook and corner of some fair harbor—for the dolphin is sure to eat all it can catch—so the Trojans cowered under the banks of the mighty river. When Achilles’s arms grew tired of killing, he drew twelve youths alive out of the water, to sacrifice in revenge for Patroclus son of Menoetius. He pulled them out like dazed fawns, tied their hands behind them with the belts of their own shirts, and handed them over to his men to take back to the ships. Then he sprang into the river again, thirsting for still more blood.
21,18: With that, the river raised his roaring flood high against Achilles. It seethed with foam, blood and the bodies of the dead. The dark waters of the river stood upright and would have overwhelmed the son of Peleus, but Hera was afraid that Achilles would be swept away in the great torrent, and she cried out loudly to her son Hephaestus. “Crook-foot,” she called, “my child, get up and act! I think it is you Xanthus wants to fight. Help us at once and light a fierce fire. Meanwhile I will bring the west wind and the white south wind up from the sea in a mighty hurricane. It will carry the flames against the heads and armor of the Trojans and burn them up. You, for your part, go along the banks of Xanthus, burning his trees and wrapping him in fire. Do not let him turn you back, whether he speaks kindly or harshly. Do not ease off until I shout to you. Then you may stop your flames.”
21,39: As he spoke, his strong hand hurled the javelin, and the spear struck Achilles on the leg below the knee. The greave of newly worked tin rang loudly, but the spear bounced off the body it had struck and did not pierce it, for the gift of the god held it back. Achilles in his turn attacked noble Agenor, but Apollo would not grant him the glory. He snatched Agenor away and hid him in a thick mist, sending him out of the battle unharmed. Then he cleverly drew the son of Peleus away from pursuing the army. He took on the likeness of Agenor and stood in front of Achilles, who ran toward him to chase him. Achilles pursued him over the grain fields of the plain, turning him toward the deep waters of the river Scamander. Apollo ran only a little way ahead and tricked Achilles, making him think the whole time that he was about to overtake him. Meanwhile the rabble of routed Trojans was glad to crowd into the city until it was packed with them. They no longer dared to wait for one another outside the walls, to learn who had escaped and who had fallen in the fight. All whose feet and knees could still carry them poured into the town in a heap.
22,6: “Alas,” he said to himself, with a heavy heart, “if I go inside the gates, Polydamas will be the first to heap reproach on me. He was the one who urged me to lead the Trojans back to the city on that awful night when Achilles came out against us again. I would not listen, though it would have been far better if I had. Now my folly has destroyed the army, and I dare not look Trojan men and Trojan women in the face, for fear that a worse man might say, ‘Hector has ruined us by his self-confidence.’ Surely it would be better for me to go back after fighting Achilles and killing him, or else to die gloriously here in front of the city. But what if I were to lay down my shield and helmet, lean my spear against the wall, and walk straight up to noble Achilles? What if I promised to give up Helen, who was the source of all this war, and all the treasure that Paris brought to Troy in his ships, and even to let the Achaeans divide half of everything the city holds? I might make the Trojans, through their princes, swear a solemn oath that they would hide nothing, and would split everything inside the city into two shares. But why argue with myself like this? If I went up to him, he would show me no mercy at all. Once I had taken off my armor, he would kill me on the spot as easily as if I were a woman. There is no talking with him from behind some rock or oak tree, the way young men and maidens chatter with one another. It is better to fight him at once, and find out which of us Zeus will grant victory.”
22,23: Achilles glared at him and answered, “Dog, do not talk to me of knees or parents. I wish I could be as sure of having the strength to cut your flesh into pieces and eat it raw, for the harm you have done me, as I am that nothing will save you from the dogs. It will not happen, though they bring ten or twenty times the ransom and weigh it out for me on the spot, with a promise of more to come. Even if Priam son of Dardanus tells them to offer me your weight in gold, your mother will still never lay you out and mourn the son she bore. Dogs and vultures will eat you up completely.”
22,29: So the head of Hector was dishonored in the dust. His mother tore her hair and flung her veil away with a loud cry when she saw her son. His father groaned piteously, and all through the city the people began to weep and wail. It was as if the whole of frowning Ilium were smoldering in fire. The people could hardly hold Priam back, so hot was his haste to rush out of the city gates. He groveled in the mire and begged them, calling each one by name. “Let it be, my friends,” he cried, “and for all your sorrow, allow me to go alone to the ships of the Achaeans. Let me plead with this cruel and terrible man. Perhaps he will respect the feelings of his fellow men and have pity on my old age. His own father is just such another as I am—Peleus, who bred him and raised him to be the bane of us Trojans, and of me more than of all others. He has killed many a son of mine in the flower of his youth. Yet however I grieve for those, I grieve for one—Hector—more than for them all, and the bitterness of my sorrow will bring me down to the house of Hades. I wish he had died in my arms. Then both his ill-starred mother who bore him and I would have had the comfort of weeping and mourning over him.”
22,30: So he spoke with many tears, and all the people of the city joined in his lament. Then Hecuba started the cry of wailing among the Trojans. “Alas, my son,” she cried, “what do I have left to live for, now that you are gone? Night and day I took glory in you throughout the city. You were a tower of strength to everyone in Troy, and men and women alike hailed you as a god. While you lived you were their pride, but now death and destruction have come upon you.”
23,2: They all broke into a wail, and Achilles led their lament. Three times they drove their chariots around the body in sorrow, and Thetis stirred a deeper longing to weep in every one of them. The sand of the shore and the men’s armor were wet with tears, so great a source of fear was the man they had lost. The son of Peleus mourned above them all. He laid his blood-stained hand on his friend’s chest and cried out: “Farewell, Patroclus, even in the house of Hades. Now I will do everything I promised you earlier. I will drag Hector here and let the dogs eat him raw. And before your pyre I will kill twelve noble sons of the Trojans, to avenge you.”
23,3: With these words he treated the body of noble Hector shamefully, stretching it out in the dust beside the bier of Patroclus. Then the others took off their armor, unhitched the horses from their chariots, and sat down in a great crowd beside the ship of the swift descendant of Aeacus. He gave them a rich funeral feast. They slaughtered and cut up many fine oxen, and many sheep and bleating goats. They also singed many fat, well-fed tusked boars and set them to roast in the flames of Hephaestus. Streams of blood ran all around the place where the body lay.
23,9: He stretched out his arms toward the spirit as he spoke and tried to hold it, but there was nothing there. The spirit vanished like vapor, gibbering and whining, into the earth. Achilles sprang to his feet and struck his hands together. He cried out in grief: “It is true, then. Even in the house of Hades there are ghosts and phantoms with no life in them. All night long the sad spirit of Patroclus has hovered over my head, moaning pitifully, telling me what I must do for him, and looking amazingly like himself.”
23,19: So he spoke, and they obeyed the son of Peleus. First they poured red wine on the thick layer of ashes and put out the fire. With many tears they picked out the whitened bones of their beloved comrade and laid them in a golden urn in two layers of fat. They covered the urn with a linen cloth and took it inside the tent. They marked out the circle for the mound, laid a foundation for it around the pyre, and at once heaped up the earth. When they had raised the mound, they were going away, but Achilles kept the people there and made them sit in assembly. He brought prizes from the ships: cauldrons, tripods, horses and mules, noble oxen, women with fair girdles, and dark iron.
23,45: With that he handed the mare to Noemon, the comrade of Antilochus, and took the cauldron for himself. Meriones had come in fourth, and he carried off the two talents of gold. The fifth prize, the two-handled urn, was still unclaimed, so Achilles gave it to Nestor. He went up to the old man among the gathered Argives and said, “Take this, my good old friend, as an heirloom and a memorial of the funeral of Patroclus, for you will not see him again among the Argives. I give you this prize though you cannot win one. You can no longer wrestle or fight, you cannot enter the javelin match or the foot races, because age has laid its heavy hand on you.”
24,19: Priam and his servant carefully saw to the yoking of their vehicles at the palace. Then Hecuba came up to them, heavy with sorrow, carrying a golden goblet of wine in her right hand so that they could pour a drink-offering before leaving. She stopped in front of the horses and said, “Take this and pour a drink-offering to father Zeus. You are determined to go to the ships against my wishes, so pray that you return safely from the hands of your enemies. Pray to the son of Cronus, lord of the whirlwind, who sits on Ida and looks down over all Troy. Ask him to send his swift messenger to your right, the bird of omen that is strongest and dearest to him of all birds, so that you see it with your own eyes and can trust it as you set out for the ships of the Danaans. If all-seeing Zeus will not send you this messenger, then however set on going you may be, I would not have you approach the ships of the Argives.”
24,20: Priam answered, “Wife, I will do as you ask. It is good to lift hands in prayer to Zeus, in the hope that he may have mercy on me.”
24,26: When the old man heard this, his heart failed him and he was in great fear. He stayed where he was as if dazed, and the hair stood on end all over his body. But the bringer of good luck came up, took him by the hand, and said, “Where, father, are you driving your mules and horses like this, in the dead of night, when other men are asleep? Are you not afraid of the fierce Achaeans, so cruel and relentless, who are close by? If one of them saw you carrying so much treasure through the darkness of the fleeting night, what would become of you? You are no longer young, and the man with you is too old to protect you from those who would attack you. As for me, I will do you no harm, and I will defend you against anyone else, for you remind me of my own father.”
24,37: When a cruel blow of fate has made a man kill someone in his own country, and he has to flee to a great man’s protection in a land of strangers, everyone who sees him is amazed. Achilles was amazed in just that way when he saw Priam. The others looked at one another in amazement too. Then Priam begged Achilles, saying, “Think of your father, Achilles, you who are like the gods. He is as old as I am, standing on the sad threshold of old age. Perhaps his neighbors are harassing him, and there is no one to keep war and ruin away from him. Yet when he hears that you are still alive, he is glad, and every day he hopes to see his dear son come home to him from Troy. But I am a wretched man. I had the bravest sons in all Troy, and not one of them is left. I had fifty sons when the Achaeans came here. Nineteen of them came from a single womb, and the others were borne to me by the women of my household. Fierce Ares has laid most of them low. Hector was the only one left, the guardian of our city and of ourselves, and you killed him not long ago. That is why I have now come to the ships of the Achaeans, to ransom his body from you with a great ransom. Fear the anger of heaven, Achilles. Think of your own father and pity me. I am more pitiable than he, because I have steeled myself as no man on earth has ever done before me. I have raised to my lips the hand of the man who killed my son.”
24,41: The old man was afraid of him and obeyed. Then the son of Peleus sprang out through the door of his house like a lion. He did not go alone. His two squires, Automedon and Alcimus, went with him. Now that Patroclus was dead, he valued these two above all his other comrades. They unyoked the horses and mules, and told Priam’s herald and attendant to sit inside the house. They lifted the ransom for Hector’s body down from the wagon, but left two mantles and a fine shirt for Achilles to wrap the body in when it was given back to be taken home. Then Achilles called to his servants and told them to wash the body and anoint it. First he took it himself to a place where Priam could not see it. He was afraid that Priam, seeing it, might break out in the bitterness of his grief and enrage him, so that he would kill the old man and sin against the word of Zeus. When the servants had washed and anointed the body and wrapped it in a fair shirt and mantle, Achilles himself lifted it onto a bier, and he and his men laid it on the wagon. As he did so he cried aloud and called on his dear comrade by name. “Do not be angry with me, Patroclus,” he said, “if you learn, even in the house of Hades, that I gave Hector back to his father for a ransom. It was not an unworthy one, and I will share it with you fairly.”
24,47: As he spoke he laid his hand on the old man’s right wrist, as a sign that he should have no fear. So Priam and his attendant slept there in the forecourt, their minds full of thought. Achilles lay in an inner room of the house, with fair Briseis beside him.
